newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Caspian Pipeline group restructuring delayed again.
newsitem.headline: Caspian Pipeline group restructuring delayed again.

text.p: The Caspian Pipeline Consortium, trying to build an oil pipeline from Kazakhstan to Russia, will extend its restructuring process by one month, and new shareholders may come on board, a CPC source said on Friday.

The source, who declined to be identified, said the group was due to finalise restructuring documents on Friday, but that the Kremlin cabinet reshuffle had delayed the signing of unspecified Russian and Kazakh governmental decrees needed to push the $2 billion project to the development stage.
"Nothing's being signed today," the source said. "There was a target date and we missed it, but we're going forward."

On the decrees, he said only that "there are certain commitments we need from the two governments before we can proceed" and that the texts of the documents were making their way through various ministries.
CPC shareholders would agree to extend the restructuring period by about a month, he said.

Chevron Corp owns 15 percent of CPC, Russia's LUKoil LKOH.RTS 12.5 percent, Mobil Corp and Russia's Rosneft 7.5 percent each, British Gas Plc and Italy's Agip SpA two percent each, and Oryx Energy Company and Kazakhstan's Munaigaz 1.75 percent each.
The remaining 50 percent is divided between Russia (24 percent), Kazakhstan (19 percent) and Oman (seven percent).
The role of Transneft -- the Russian oil pipeline monopoly that will be project operator but which wants the Russian government stake -- has been a key negotiating sticking point.
"I've heard rumours it (the stake) has been transferred to Transneft, but I haven't seen any documents to confirm this," the source said.
Transneft spokesman Ravil Polyanin said he expected the monopoly to receive the stake but that a government decision on the matter had been delayed by the cabinet reshuffle.

CPC was working out what the source called adequate conditions to deal with the possibility of Transneft as the biggest shareholder, adding, "if you're going to get married, you want a prenuptial agreement."

CPC will build a 1,580 km (990 mile) pipeline from Kazakhstan's Tengiz oil field to Russia's Black Sea oil export outlet Novorossiisk. Chevron and Mobil, with their $20 billion Tengiz project, are CPC's main future customers, but other producers will be granted access.

Questions have been raised over whether Amoco Corp of the United States -- which recently signed a $150 million deal with Almaty to finance Kazakhstan's state share in the project -- will take a formal stake in CPC.

"If Texaco has a piece of Karachaganak (a $10 billion Kazakh oil and gas project), then maybe they'd like a piece of BritGas's and Agip's (CPC) stake," the source said, adding that such questions were mere speculation at this point.
Texaco bought 20 percent of Karachaganak by acquiring parts of stakes held by British Gas and Agip in the project.
CPC, set up in 1992, plans a pipeline with an initial capacity of 28 million tonnes a year (560,000 barrels per day) and a peak of 67 million tonnes a year (1.34 million bpd).
